title: Building a Career with Purpose: A Professional's Perspective

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Alieva
dialogue.text: Good morning, everyone. I'm going to talk today about something that I think gets too little attention in career guidance: how to build a career that is genuinely yours — one that aligns with your values, plays to your strengths, and contributes something you care about.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Alieva
dialogue.text: Let me start with a distinction I find essential. There is a difference between a job, a career, and a calling. A job is what you do for money. A career is a sequence of jobs with a direction — a sense of progression and accumulation of expertise. A calling is work that you feel you were meant to do — work that connects to your deepest values and sense of purpose.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Alieva
dialogue.text: Most people operate at the job or career level. Very few reach the level of calling — and those who do often describe it not as a discovery but as a gradual construction. They did not find their calling; they built it, through years of developing skills, exploring interests, and making choices that brought them progressively closer to work they found deeply meaningful.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Alieva
dialogue.text: This distinction matters because much career advice tells young people to "follow their passion." The research, however, suggests this advice is often counterproductive. Passion is not something you discover fully-formed in yourself and then apply to a career. It tends to follow mastery — the better you become at something, the more interesting and engaging it becomes. So the most reliable path to meaningful work is often not to follow your passion, but to develop your skills until you become genuinely excellent at something, and then to use that excellence in service of something you care about.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Alieva
dialogue.text: A second insight from the research is the importance of what I call "career experiments." Rather than making one large, irreversible decision about your career direction — which is rarely necessary and often paralyses people — I encourage you to run small experiments. Take on a project in a new area. Volunteer for a role that stretches you. Have conversations with people in fields you find interesting. Treat your early career as a period of deliberate exploration rather than a race to a fixed destination.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Alieva
dialogue.text: Third, and perhaps most importantly: your career is not just about what you do — it is about who you become. The skills you develop, the habits of mind you cultivate, the relationships you build, the values you embody in your work — these are the real outputs of a career. They outlast any particular job title or employer. They are yours, and they compound over time.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Alieva
dialogue.text: I want to close by challenging a notion that I encounter constantly: the idea that ambition is about winning — about beating others, reaching the top, accumulating status and recognition. The ambition I admire is different. It is the quiet, persistent drive to get better at something, to contribute something real, and to do so with integrity. That kind of ambition is not zero-sum. There is no limit to how many people can have it. And it tends, in my experience, to be the kind that actually produces a life worth looking back on.
